title: The one who spreads and gathers
hook: the Creator spreads creation out and draws it back into Himself (Chaupai)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sevak sikh, and your line, carry them across. Did you send that friend a message? Today Chaupai widens all the way, to the whole of creation. Day three hundred seventy-five.

Watch a jellyfish move. It opens, wide and slow, like an umbrella, and then it closes, pulling itself in, and in that closing it moves forward. Open, close. Spread out, gather in. Or watch your own chest for a few seconds. It's doing the same thing. Out, in. Out, in. Lungs, tides, seasons, a beating heart. A huge amount of the living world runs on that one rhythm. Chaupai takes that rhythm and applies it to the biggest thing there is. Today: kartaar.
screen: `A JELLYFISH OPENS AND CLOSES.` → `OUT, IN. LUNGS, TIDES, A HEART.` → `THE RHYTHM AT THE BIGGEST SCALE.`

segments.voice: In the middle of Chaupai, the prayer stops asking for a moment and simply looks at God. In paraphrase: when the Creator spreads creation out, beings take bodies beyond number. And when, at any time, you draw it back in, all bodies merge back into you. The two old words are udkarakh, spreading out, and aakarakh, drawing in. Out, and in. The whole universe, in this picture, is the Creator's long breath. Breathe out, and there are galaxies, rivers, people, ants. Breathe in, and everything returns to the One it came from. That's a big idea, and it echoes something you met in the Japji. Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that with a single word the Creator made the vast expanse, and from it a million rivers flowed. Creation in Sikh thought isn't a machine built once and left to run. It flows out of the One, and it's held in the One the whole time. Now, why is this in a prayer for protection? Because it changes what being kept means. If everything came out of the One and returns to the One, then nothing that happens to you happens outside God. Even the drawing in, the ending of things, which frightens us most, is described as merging, not vanishing. Bodies merge back into you. That doesn't make loss painless. Sikhs grieve like everyone else. But it puts the loss inside something larger and kinder. The same hand that spread you out is the hand that gathers you in. And the line asks you to see your own breath as a small copy of that.
screen: `THE PRAYER STOPS ASKING AND LOOKS.` · `UDKARAKH: SPREADING OUT.` · `AAKARAKH: DRAWING BACK IN.` · `EVEN THE ENDING IS MERGING.` · then, large: `SPREAD AND GATHERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe out, then in. Start with the out-breath. Let it go long and slow, all the way, as if you're spreading something out into the room. Pause for a beat. Then let the in-breath come by itself, gathering back. Do that again. Out, spreading. In, gathering. Don't force the rhythm. Let it be the rhythm your body already knows. If you pray, you can let Waheguru ride on the breath, wahe on the way out, guru on the way in. If you don't, just watch the two halves of each breath. The bell holds the time.
Kartaar, the Creator. Udkarakh and aakarakh: spreading creation out into countless bodies, and drawing it all back to merge in the One.
Your line: spread and gathered. Today, each time you step through a doorway, take one slow breath out and one in, and remember the bigger breath it copies. Day three hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite these verses of Chaupai Sahib daily, and Sikh teaching describes creation as flowing out from the One and merging back into the One.

match.prompt: spread and gathered — tap the pairs.

myth: in Chaupai, the drawing in of creation means everything simply vanishes
the verse says all bodies merge back into the One.
the Japji also pictures creation flowing from the Creator's single word
Guru Nanak says one word made the vast expanse, and rivers flowed from it.
Sikh thought pictures creation as a machine built once and left alone
it flows out of the One and stays held in the One the whole time.

fork.setup: Chaupai says the Creator spreads creation out into bodies beyond number. what does it say happens when the Creator draws it back in?
options: all bodies merge back into the One.
fork.reveal: jab aakarakh karat ho kabahoon, tum mai milat deh dhar sabhahoon: when you draw it in, all who took bodies merge into you.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kartaar, the Creator, the one Chaupai pictures spreading creation out and gathering it in.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about the end of the world.
what it means: the whole universe as the Creator's breath: spread out into countless bodies, gathered back to merge in the One.
what a scholar hears: the pair udkarakh and aakarakh, expansion and contraction, gives Chaupai a cosmology of emanation and return, in step with the Japji's picture of one word making the expanse.

sources.ref: Benti Chaupai (Chaupai Sahib), verse 'jab udkarakh karaa kartaaraa'
sources.quoted: jab aakarakh karat ho kabahoon, tum mai milat deh dhar sabhahoon

sources.ref: Japji, pauri 16 (one word, the vast expanse)

notes: Verse paraphrased: 'jab udkarakh karaa kartaaraa, prajaa dharat tab deh apaaraa; jab aakarakh karat ho kabahoon, tum mai milat deh dhar sabhahoon'. The fork reveal quotes the second half in transliteration. Confirm transliteration and meaning.
Japji pauri 16 ('keetaa pasaao eko kavaao, tis te hoe lakh dareeaao') paraphrased; confirm pauri number and Ang 3.
The breath picture for udkarakh/aakarakh is an illustration; the verse itself does not use the word breath. Confirm acceptable.
Wahe on the out-breath, guru on the in-breath: offered as an option; some Sikh practice pairs the syllables with breath, but customs differ. Confirm.
